takehome-01-shortener:
# Shortener

A URL shortener written in Go, with SQLite for storage.

Run it with `make run`. Tests run with `make test`.

Short codes are random 7-character base62 strings. If a code collides I retry up to three times, then return a 500.

There's no authentication or rate limiting, and I haven't run any load tests.
takehome-02-limiter:
I used a token bucket in Python, with Redis holding the state. A Lua script keeps each check atomic, and it uses Redis time, so clock skew between app servers isn't a problem. The limit is 100 requests per minute per API key.

If Redis goes down, the limiter fails open. I'd rather not lose the API to a Redis outage, but limits won't be enforced while it's down.

This took about five hours.
takehome-03-ingest:
This is a Python and DuckDB pipeline for the orders CSV. It got through 2.1 million rows in 38 seconds on my laptop. I haven't tried it on a production-sized file.

Duplicates are removed by order_id, keeping the row with the latest updated_at. 1,204 malformed rows went to quarantine.csv.

One known bug: a name that isn't valid UTF-8 fails the whole run.
takehome-04-kanban:
# Kanban board

Built with React and TypeScript. State lives in Zustand and drag and drop uses dnd-kit.

Start it with `npm run dev`.

Card moves are optimistic, so the UI updates right away and rolls back if the API call fails.

Keyboard dragging doesn't work yet, and that's what I'd do next. There's no offline support either.

takehome-06-logsearch:
# logq

A small Rust command-line tool for searching JSON log files.

Install it with `cargo install --path .`, then run something like:

    logq app.log --level error --since 1h

It streams each file line by line, so memory stays flat even on big logs. On my laptop it searched a 4 GB file in about 9 seconds.

It can't read gzipped files yet, and I haven't tested Windows paths.
takehome-07-jobqueue:
## Design notes

This is a background job queue in Node.js, using Postgres as the store. Workers claim jobs with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so several workers can pull from the same table without grabbing the same job.

A failed job retries up to 5 times with exponential backoff. After that it moves to a dead-letter table.

A job can run twice if a worker crashes after finishing it but before marking it done, so handlers need to be idempotent.

I picked Postgres over Redis so there's one less service to run. With 4 workers it topped out near 800 jobs per second in my benchmark.
takehome-08-churn:
## Churn model

I trained a LightGBM model on the 48,000-customer subscription dataset. It reaches a ROC AUC of 0.81 on the held-out test set, against 0.74 for logistic regression.

I split the data by customer and by time, so no customer appears in both train and test. The strongest features were days since last login and support tickets in the last 30 days.

I dropped `cancellation_reason`, because it only gets filled in after a customer churns.

The model isn't calibrated, so treat its scores as a ranking, not as probabilities.
takehome-09-loans:
# Library loans API

A REST API for book loans, built with FastAPI and Postgres.

Start everything with `docker compose up`, then open http://localhost:8000/docs for the interactive docs. Run the tests with `pytest`.

A member can't take out a new loan if they already have 5 active loans. Migrations use Alembic.

Auth is a single hard-coded API key. That's fine for this exercise but not for real use. The list endpoints don't have pagination yet.

takehome-11-chat:
## Design notes

The chat server is written in Elixir with Phoenix Channels. Each room runs in its own process, so a crash in one room doesn't take down the others.

Messages are saved to Postgres before they're broadcast. That adds about 15 ms of latency, but nothing is lost if the server restarts. Typing indicators are broadcast but never stored.

I tested 2,000 concurrent connections on one machine.

There's no end-to-end encryption, and messages are stored in plain text.
takehome-12-expenses:
# Expenses

An expense tracker built with React Native and Expo.

Run `npx expo start` and scan the QR code with the Expo Go app.

Everything is stored on the device in SQLite, so it works offline. Receipt photos are compressed to under 500 KB before they're saved.

I tested it on an iPhone 13 and a Pixel 7. The Android back button on the edit screen is buggy, and there's no cloud sync.
takehome-13-bikeshare:
## Summary

This notebook looks at 1.3 million bike-share trips from 2023, using pandas.

Weekday rides peak at 8am and 5pm. On weekends the peak is around 2pm.

Members take shorter trips than casual riders, with a median of 11 minutes against 19.

Rainy days had about 40% fewer trips. I could only match weather for 280 of the 365 days, and this shows the two move together, not that rain causes the drop.

The notebook runs top to bottom in about 3 minutes.
takehome-14-pricecache:
## Notes

This is a read-through cache in Go that sits in front of the slow pricing API. Entries expire after 60 seconds, and concurrent requests for the same key collapse into one upstream call with singleflight.

The cache lives in memory on each instance, so two instances can briefly return different prices.

In my load test with 200 users, p95 latency dropped from 420 ms to 35 ms.

I didn't implement invalidation when prices change, so a price can be up to 60 seconds stale.
